title: Edmund and the Harvest
premise: Felix Ashgrove, a late-night radio host, begins receiving calls from listeners who died the previous week—each humming the same half-remembered harvest song. When every photograph from his late grandmother's house shows an extra empty chair, Felix returns to the village of Hollowmere, where the song's final verse was deliberately cut from the town's memory after a 1923 harvest ritual that fed the fields with the dead. The song is a covenant: someone must sing the last verse each generation, or the fields take their payment themselves. Felix must learn the verse from the ghost-choir without singing along, expose the founding families who've been choosing sacrifices for a century, and end the covenant—but the song, once fully heard, wants a voice, and Felix's is the only one left that fits.
about_author: Gideon Voss is the pen name of a former small-town radio engineer who spent a decade maintaining transmitter towers in farming country before turning to fiction. Their work draws on rural folklore, dead-air silences, and the unsettling intimacy of voices on the airwaves.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Felix, hosting the graveyard shift at community station KLMR, takes a call from a devoted listener—and realizes mid-conversation she died six days ago. The call log shows no caller ID, no duration, nothing. Felix convinces himself it's a prank, but the woman's final words, a hummed melody, lodge in his head. POV Felix. Beat: denial cracking open into dread.

chapters.title: The Second Caller
chapters.summary: Two nights later, a man calls asking Felix to 'tell Marta the verse isn't her fault' before dissolving into static. Felix researches Marta and finds an obituary: same week, same village his grandmother came from—Hollowmere. He begins recording every call. POV Felix. Beat: the denial collapses; obsession takes root.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Boxes
chapters.summary: Sorting his late grandmother Edith's house, Felix notices every photograph—decades of family pictures—now includes one extra empty wooden chair that wasn't there when taken. His cousin Priya, who grew up in Hollowmere, refuses to discuss it and begs him not to go back. POV Felix. Beat: the past stops being past.

chapters.title: Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Felix drives to the village, finding it prosperous in a wrong way—immaculate fields, no children, doors that close as he passes. The extra chair appears in his rearview mirror's reflection of the back seat. He checks into the only inn and hears, faintly, singing from the direction of the wheat. POV Felix. Beat: isolation and first true fear.

chapters.title: The Harvest Board
chapters.summary: Felix visits the Hollowmere Historical Society and meets archivist Ruth Calloway, who recognizes Edith's name and goes pale. The town records show a suspicious gap: all documents between 1923 and 1931 are missing. Ruth warns him, quietly, to leave before 'the Board' notices him. POV Felix. Beat: first ally, first warning.

chapters.title: Chair Number Nine
chapters.summary: In Edith's old cottage, Felix finds nine chairs arranged around a bare table and a hymnal with the harvest song's final verse razored out, the stubs of the page left like teeth. That night the ghost-choir sings in the field; he recognizes the dead callers' voices among them. POV Felix. Beat: the supernatural becomes undeniable.

chapters.title: What Marta Knew
chapters.summary: Felix contacts Marta's sister, Del, a Hollowmere expatriate, who reveals the covenant: in 1923 the founding families bound the fields with a sung pact, and every generation someone must sing the last verse—giving a life to the harvest. Edith was the last singer; Felix is the next in line. POV Del (letter/phone). Beat: the rules of the horror are named.

chapters.title: The Board Notices
chapters.summary: Chairman Aldous Vane invites Felix to dinner, courteous and chilling, offering him a place in Hollowmere's 'family.' Felix realizes Vane's family has chosen the singer for a century—always someone expendable, never a Vane. POV Felix. Beat: the human villain emerges; power's corruption made polite.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth admits she's been archiving the Board's victims in secret for thirty years—names, dates, the song fragments she's forbidden to write down. She gives Felix a wax cylinder recording of Edith singing, made the week before her death. The recording ends mid-word. POV Ruth. Beat: guilt, complicity, and the weight of witness.

chapters.title: The Cylinder
chapters.summary: Playing the cylinder at the cottage, Felix hears Edith's warning woven into the melody: the song can be ended, not just passed on, if the last verse is heard whole by someone who never sings it. But the choir in the field grows louder each night, and one chair at the table is no longer empty—it holds his shape. POV Felix. Beat: hope and a deadline.

chapters.title: Priya Arrives
chapters.summary: Priya shows up unannounced, furious and terrified, revealing she left Hollowmere at seventeen after being chosen as the next singer—Edith took her place instead. She's spent her life running, and she's brought the one thing she stole: the razored verse fragment. POV Priya. Beat: found family forms; guilt and love collide.

chapters.title: The Choir's Bargain
chapters.summary: The dead callers reach Felix through the radio he brought—a voice offers him Edith's place in the choir if he walks into the field tonight, painless, 'already sung.' Felix, exhausted and grieving, nearly goes; Priya drags him back from the treeline at dawn. POV Felix. Beat: the lowest moment—temptation of surrender.

chapters.title: Vane's Ledger
chapters.summary: Felix and Priya break into the Board's hall and find the ledger: a century of chosen singers, each entry in Vane's hand, each sacrifice a poor, childless, or friendless soul—never a founding family. The corruption isn't the fields'; it's the men who fed them. POV Felix. Beat: righteous anger; justice outside the law takes shape.

chapters.title: The Fields Remember
chapters.summary: The covenant, insulted by the theft of the ledger, turns on the town itself: wheat rises in walls, the harvest comes early, and Board members begin hearing the song in their own houses. Vane begs Felix to sing, offering anything. Felix refuses—this is not his debt alone. POV Aldous Vane. Beat: power devours its holders.

chapters.title: Ruth's Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Ruth commandeers KLMR's transmitter and broadcasts the ledger to the county, naming every chosen singer and every signer. Half of Hollowmere flees; the rest gather at the field with torches, some to end the covenant, some to protect it. Ruth is taken by the Board—but the truth is loose. POV Ruth. Beat: sacrifice; the town fractures.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: At Edith's cottage the table now seats the whole choir, Edith among them, the ninth chair waiting for Felix. She cannot speak, but she shows him: the verse razored out was not a protection—it was a lock, and the Board holds the key page in the hall's foundation stone. POV Felix (dream/vision). Beat: understanding; the plan crystallizes.

chapters.title: Foundation Stone
chapters.summary: Felix and Priya dig up the foundation stone at dawn, recovering the original 1923 verse in the founders' hands—written to be sung by proxy, never by the signers themselves. Vane and his remnant confront them at the field's edge as the harvest-dark gathers. Standoff, blades, and the choir rising behind them all. POV Priya. Beat: the climax begins.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Vane forces the confrontation: sing and live as the Board's warden, or the fields take Hollowmere entire. Felix chooses a third path—he reads the verse aloud, never singing it, giving the covenant its words without a voice to bind. The song, incomplete, turns on those who made it. POV Felix. Beat: the climax—the refusal that breaks the pattern.

chapters.title: What the Wheat Took
chapters.summary: The fields reclaim their debt from the founding families, Vane last, dragged singing into the wheat in a voice that is suddenly, horribly his own. The choir, freed of the covenant's terms, does not vanish—but the hunger does. Edith's chair empties last, and she smiles. POV Felix. Beat: catharsis; justice done by no court.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: The county arrives to find a village half-empty, a ledger, and two survivors who tell a story no one fully believes and no one fully disbelieves. The photographs from Edith's house now show the table bare. Felix buries the hymnal and the verse page in unmarked ground. POV Felix. Beat: exhaustion, grief, the strange peace of survival.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Felix returns to the night shift at KLMR. The dead no longer call—but one night, a listener phones in to request 'that harvest song,' and Felix, smiling, plays something else instead, then talks with her until sunrise about nothing important at all. POV Felix. Beat: healing; the found family of the airwaves endures.

chapters.title: The Verse Unwritten
chapters.summary: Epilogue: Priya, staying in Hollowmere to help the town rebuild, finds the field quiet and green, the wheat ordinary at last. In the historical society, Ruth's archive is made public. And in Felix's last photograph of the cottage, for the first time in a century, there is one chair fewer than there should be. POV Priya. Beat: resolution—the debt paid, the door closed.
